issues.description: The entire analysis pipeline depends on isolating 'high confidence' trials, yet the manuscript never specifies the cutoff used to dichotomize the 4-point confidence scale (e.g., whether 'high confidence' means only rating 4, or ratings 3-4). This is a critical undisclosed researcher degree of freedom because the central claim (illusions occur with high confidence) and all exclusion decisions hinge on this threshold. Different cutoffs could materially change which trials and participants are retained and the reported error rates.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain).

issues.subcategory: high exclusion rate / selection on outcome-related variable
issues.description: Participants were excluded for having too few high-confidence trials, removing 17/40 (42.5%) in Exp 1 and 92/290 (31.7%) in Exp 2. Because exclusion is based on how often participants use high confidence ratings—a variable directly tied to the dependent measure (high-confidence illusions)—the retained sample is systematically biased toward confident responders, who may be more prone to high-confidence errors. This conditioning on a post-treatment, outcome-correlated variable threatens the validity of the reported illusion rates.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: evidence of selection bias between included/excluded groups
issues.description: Included and excluded participants differ dramatically on the very dimension used for selection (e.g., 53.8% vs 26.2% high-confidence trials in Exp 1; 49.2% vs 15.7% in Exp 2). This confirms that exclusion produced a non-random subsample. No sensitivity analysis (e.g., reanalysis with a lower trial threshold or full sample) is reported to show the effects are robust to this selection.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 53.8% high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: 36.3 – 93.2, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.subcategory: uncontrolled stimulus parameters in online testing
issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online via participants' own laptops, yet stimuli are specified in degrees of visual angle (inherited from Exp 2/3). Online, viewing distance, monitor size, and resolution are uncontrolled, so the carefully specified retinal sizes, luminances (CIE/cd/m2), and timing cannot be guaranteed. This undermines comparability with the lab-based experiments whose results are pooled with it.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.description: The text states the increase in illusory errors was 'smaller' for mirrored targets while simultaneously reporting a larger numeric value for mirrored (5%) than for real-letter targets (4%). A 5% increase is not smaller than a 4% increase, so either the wording or the numbers are wrong. This contradiction obscures the actual pattern of the (non-supported) three-way interaction.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: In the Experiment 4 results, the figure is referred to as 'Figure 5', but Figure 5 is the Experiment 3 figure; the Experiment 4 figure is Figure 6. This mislabeling could mislead readers comparing reported values to the displayed data.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: In Table 1, the BFincl for Target Type and Error Type are reported as exactly identical (1.462e+14, with identical P(incl|data) and P(excl|data)), and in Table 6 the Target Type and Error Type values are again exactly identical (1.97e+13). Two conceptually distinct effects yielding identical inclusion Bayes factors to four significant figures is statistically implausible and suggests a copy/paste or computational error in the tables.

Experiments 3 and 4 used a sequential stopping rule (stop when BF for the critical test crosses 10), checked every other testing day. While optional stopping is more defensible in a Bayesian framework, the procedure introduces researcher degrees of freedom (e.g., the chosen threshold, the choice of which single test drives stopping, the checking interval) and no pre-registration is cited. Stopping when evidence crosses a favorable threshold can inflate apparent effect magnitudes.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: world-knowledge conclusion not directly supported by manipulation
issues.description: The 'world knowledge' account is inferred from the pseudo-to-real vs real-to-pseudo asymmetry (a correlational pattern), but the only direct experimental manipulation of expectations (the colored-cue contingency in Exp 2) produced a null result. Attributing the asymmetry specifically to lifelong 'world knowledge' rather than other correlates (e.g., perceptual fluency, lexical/representational strength of real letters, decisional familiarity) is therefore an inference from an unmanipulated variable, not a demonstrated causal driver.
issues.quote: However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories.

issues.description: The failure of the transient cue manipulation is interpreted as evidence that 'expectations need substantial time to develop.' This is one of several explanations; the null could equally reflect a weak/undetected contingency (participants showed no awareness of it and may never have learned it), insufficient power for the implicit-learning effect, or an inappropriate manipulation. Drawing a positive theoretical conclusion from a null is not warranted.
issues.quote: This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.description: The dependent variable is the relative occurrence of response types (illusory errors, other errors, correct), which are bounded proportions that are mutually constrained (they are parts of a whole within each cell). Standard repeated-measures ANOVA assumes unbounded, normally distributed, independent observations. Non-independence among the proportions (an increase in one category necessarily constrains others) can distort effect estimates and interactions, and is not addressed.
issues.quote: error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: sample limitation and extrapolation to sensory processing in general
issues.description: Samples are predominantly young first-year psychology students from one Dutch university, tested with Latin-alphabet stimuli, yet the conclusions are generalized to memory/perception of 'sensory input' in general. The leap from overlearned letter stimuli in a WEIRD undergraduate sample to a universal feature of cognitive processing is an overclaim that is not tempered by acknowledgment of sample or stimulus constraints.
issues.quote: This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.subcategory: trial-by-trial feedback may alter the phenomenon
issues.description: Participants received correct/incorrect feedback after every trial and were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters. Feedback indicating that real/pseudo confusions are errors could plausibly reduce, induce, or otherwise reshape the very illusions under study (e.g., via learning or demand), and feedback differences across experiments are not discussed as a potential moderator of the cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.description: Experiment 3 reports inclusion of 59 participants after exclusions, but then states an additional participant was removed from the main ANOVA via listwise deletion, implying an effective N of 58. The actual sample size entering the primary analysis is therefore ambiguous.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 59 participants (5 participants were excluded). ... Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.description: Experiment 1 manipulated set size (6 vs 8) but results are 'averaged across the set size conditions' without reporting set-size-specific analyses or justifying the collapse. Set sizes also differed in the number of pseudo-letters (1-2 vs 2), so collapsing could mask set-size effects and represents an undisclosed analytic choice.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: confidence and forced-choice as index of 'illusory memory'
issues.description: The construct 'illusory memory' (a phenomenally experienced false memory trace) is operationalized as a high-confidence forced-choice selection of the mirrored alternative. High decision confidence in a 6-alternative choice need not reflect a vivid false memory; it could reflect decisional confidence, response/familiarity bias, or metacognitive miscalibration. The mapping between the measure and the claimed subjective construct is not validated.
issues.quote: isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: temporal increase does not uniquely identify trace 'conversion'
issues.description: The claim that correctly encoded percepts are 'being converted to illusory memories' during STM is one of several accounts of the time-dependent increase. An alternative the authors partly raise—differential decay, whereby correct pseudo-letter traces decay faster than prior-supported real-letter responses—could produce the same temporal increase at retrieval/decision without any in-storage 'conversion.' The authors' counterargument (uniform guessing) does not rule out differential decay, so the strong causal/mechanistic claim is underdetermined.
issues.quote: Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.description: The transient-expectation manipulation in Exp 2 set pseudo-letter target probability at 25% (red) vs 60% (blue)—an asymmetric contrast not centered on 50% and only a 35-point difference—delivered implicitly via fixation color. Given that no participant reported awareness of the contingency, the manipulation may simply have been too weak or unlearned to produce expectation effects, which weakens the inference drawn from its null result.
issues.quote: If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent probe timing reported across sections
issues.description: The General Discussion states illusions reach ~20% 'when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2),' but Experiment 1's short condition probed at 0.75 seconds (750 ms), not 500 ms. Conflating these timings misrepresents the experimental parameters when summarizing pooled effects.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.subcategory: low and unreported trial counts per analysis cell
issues.description: Because only ~13% of trials are critical for each illusion type and these are then split by delay and target type and further restricted to high-confidence responses, the number of trials contributing to each cell estimate is very small (the inclusion threshold was merely >10 per cell). Per-cell trial counts and the resulting measurement precision are not reported, making it difficult to evaluate the reliability of the cell-level percentages.
issues.quote: Together, the critical trials made up ~220 trials, 26% of all trials in the experiment.

issues.description: The three-way Target × Delay × Error interaction is treated as meaningful and decomposed in Exp 2 (BFincl=206), but is only anecdotal in Exp 1 (BFincl=2.45) and shows evidence against inclusion in Exp 4 (BFincl=0.45). This inconsistency in the key higher-order pattern across nominally replicating designs is not reconciled, and the elaborate follow-up decomposition in Exp 2 is not paralleled where the interaction is absent.
issues.quote: Memory delay had a clear effect on error rates, which depended on both error type and target type, resulting in a three-way interaction between Memory Delay, Error Type and Target Type (BFincl=206).

issues.description: The abstract and discussion claim support that 'all memory stages, including STM' integrate predictions, and that 'all stages of STM are susceptible.' However, iconic memory was not tested (the authors acknowledge this elsewhere), and only WM/fragile-memory-like timeframes were probed. The sweeping framing outruns the evidence actually collected.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions

issues.description: Experiments pooled in the conclusions differ on numerous procedural parameters (cue duration 0.5 s in Exp 1 vs 0.25 s in Exp 2-4; presence/absence of a training phase; short delay 0.75 s vs 0.5 s; lab vs online; balanced vs unbalanced stimulus sets; different sample sizes and exclusion rates). These differences are not modeled or controlled when statements like 'four experiments consistently show' are made, limiting the strength of the cumulative claim.
issues.quote: Four experiments consistently show that illusory memories can arise even when the to-be-remembered items have only just disappeared from vision.

issues.subcategory: absence of pre-registration for confirmatory hypotheses
issues.description: The introduction frames three a priori, directional hypotheses tested across four experiments, but no pre-registration of hypotheses, sample sizes, exclusion rules, the high-confidence cutoff, or analysis models is reported (only an informal sequential stopping rule for Exp 3-4). Given the many flexible choices (exclusion thresholds, collapsing factors, follow-up decompositions), the lack of pre-registration leaves substantial undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: In 4 experiments we thus test 3 hypotheses: 1) Illusions occur in STM

issues.description: The argument that response bias is ruled out rests on the claim that bias should be at least as strong on low-confidence trials. This assumes confidence is independent of the bias mechanism, but a familiarity-driven bias could itself inflate confidence (real letters feel more familiar), producing exactly the observed high-confidence asymmetry. The logic thus does not cleanly separate a 'memory illusion' from a familiarity-based decision/confidence bias.
issues.quote: the tendency to report more expectation-induced illusions than similarity induced illusions is clearly present in high confidence trials, but is much less pronounced in low confidence trials – an opposite finding to what one would expect if these effects were the result of a response bias
